verification_readings.fact: (a) executor semantics of recovery_loop's on_exhausted_status: escalated versus review_rework_loop's on_exhausted: escalation
verification_readings.detail: on_exhausted_status calls state.end(status, "'<loop>' did not converge within N iterations") and returns False — the run ends there, terminal. on_exhausted calls await self._run_from(node.on_exhausted, state) — control hands off to the named node's sub-graph. spec.py:381-384 rejects a loop that sets both. So recovery_loop ends `escalated` and review_rework_loop routes into `escalation`, exactly as the ruling states.

verification_readings.fact: (c) no graph-level bound on escalation↔recovery re-entry beyond per-loop iteration bounds
verification_readings.reads: AS RULED — and the unboundedness the ruling predicts is confirmed mechanically.
verification_readings.detail: _run_from iterates self.spec.handoff_subgraph(start_id) with no depth counter, no visited set and no budget of its own. _run_loop opens `for attempt in range(1, budget + 1)` on every call, so each fresh entry restarts the counter at 1. A routing gate inside recovery_loop targeting escalation would therefore give escalation → recoverable → recovery_loop → gate → escalation with a full iteration budget each cycle and nothing to stop it. The ruling's rationale is correct as written.

verification_readings.citation: workflows/engineering-rnd.yaml body lists; when-clause at workflows/engineering-rnd.yaml:110
verification_readings.detail: The shared body is [implement, domain_review, coverage, consistency, validate, judges, rework_review, review_fold]. Paid (kind: ai): implement, domain_review, validate, rework_review — four per iteration, with domain_review gated on `when: implement.green == true`, so three when the implementation is red. Free (kind: check): coverage, consistency, judges, review_fold. The free checks pre-empt nothing on this path, because no gate on it consumes their result to route — they feed the judges fold, which is the loop's `until` condition, not a router. So a refusal inside these loops costs three or four paid calls per iteration up to the loop bound, against zero extra on the build path where blocked_gate short-circuits before domain_review.

verification_readings.reads: READS DIFFERENTLY. This is the block.
verification_readings.detail: Three corrections to the ruling's sentence. FIRST, the trace records no verdict payload at all: StepRecord's fields are node_id, kind, iteration, skipped, reason, seconds — no blocked_on, in any loop, on any path. What carries per-iteration blocked_on is the failure_log, which is a different artifact and is read by the escalation autopsy prompt (autornd/engine/phases.py:987-1008), not by the trace. SECOND, the failure_log has two write sites and they are not equivalent. _blocked_on_unmet (adapter.py:264-289) writes an entry whenever the check fails, and that node exists only in build_loop's body. _phase_validate (adapter.py:372-382) writes an entry carrying list(getattr(implement, 'blocked_on', None) or []), and validate is in all three bodies — but that write is guarded by `if not verdict.green or not implement.green`. THIRD, and this is the consequence that matters: an implement verdict that is green and also carries blocked_on entries records NOTHING inside recovery_loop or review_rework_loop. In build_loop that same verdict routes to escalation, because blocked_check depends only on [implement], carries no when-clause, and blocked_on_unmet (checks.py:219-224) never consults green. So the asymmetry is not merely 'no short-circuit, but the record still travels'. For the green-but-blocked case the record does not travel either, and the autopsy that the ruling relies on as the rework path's protection would be diagnosing from silence — which is the exact failure mode adapter.py:267-273 documents and fixes for the build path.

blockers.what: The ruling's clause 'the per-iteration trace records blocked_on entries either way' does not hold as written. It holds for red iterations, via the validate write site. It fails for a green-but-blocked implement inside recovery_loop or review_rework_loop, where no failure-log entry is written and no gate exists to catch it.
blockers.why_it_matters: That clause is load-bearing in the ruling. It is what makes 'iteration bounds are the protection, and exhaustion ends escalated' an acceptable trade rather than a silent loss — the argument is that the refusal still reaches the autopsy. In the green-but-blocked case on those two loops it does not.
